cards.title: Three tiers of content: diagnose your library and upgrade the mix
cards.summary: Classify every piece of your store content as commodity, personality, or original, then deliberately move the mix upward.
cards.use_when: Auditing your blog, email list, or social feed to decide what to produce next and what to stop producing for an ecommerce brand.
steps: Label each existing asset: Commodity = facts anyone could publish ('drink more water', 'leather lasts longer than pleather'). Personality = tied to specific, unmade details about your brand, founders, customers, or process that nobody else has. Original = a distilled paradigm that shifts how the category thinks, typically only reachable after years of accumulated thinking.
Score your mix. If almost everything is commodity, your content competes on volume alone and is trivially replaceable by any AI or competitor.

Convert commodity pieces into personality pieces by anchoring them in specifics: swap 'how to care for leather' for the actual story of the batch that failed, the exact tannery you use, or a customer's real repair story.
Treat original content as a long-term byproduct of deep, repeated work — the source describes it as rare and category-shifting, not something you manufacture daily.
Allocate production time toward personality content (repeatable, defensible) and reserve protected time for the slow crystallization that may eventually yield original content.
caveats: The tier definitions and their rarity are the source's framework, not measured benchmarks.
Commodity content can still drive search traffic; the point is you cannot defend it, not that it has zero value.
cards.source_name: The Right Way To Write With AI.docx

cards.title: I vs. You: shift copy from second person prescription to first person experience
cards.summary: Rewriting 'You should X' as 'I did X / I think X' instantly converts generic commodity advice into personality content.
cards.use_when: Writing product descriptions, founder-story emails, category blog posts, or ad copy where the current draft reads like generic advice.
steps: Scan the draft for second-person prescriptive sentences: 'You need to...', 'You should...', 'The best way to...'.
Rewrite each one as a first-person account of what actually happened: 'I wore these boots for 40 days straight. Day 12 is when I noticed...' / 'We tried three factories before we found one that...'.
Keep the underlying lesson — the shift is not removing advice, it is grounding the advice in a tested, owned experience.
Add concrete unmade details per claim: dates, quantities, names of suppliers, specific failures, sensory specifics. Personality content is defined by details only you can supply.
On a product page, apply this to the origin/craft section and to FAQ answers; on email, use it in the opening anecdote before any offer.
Note the source's framing is a strong heuristic ('immediately'), not a universal law — second person is still appropriate for direct instructions (sizing, shipping, compliance).
caveats: Overusing first person on transactional pages (checkout, policy pages) can hurt clarity.
First person only produces personality content if the details are genuinely specific and unmade; vague I-statements are still commodity.

cards.title: Build an unmade dataset so AI remixes proprietary material, not generic slop
cards.summary: Since every LLM trains on the same public corpus, your defensible input is the manually authored record of brand-specific stories, failures, and viewpoints.
cards.use_when: Setting up how your team feeds AI writing tools for product content, email copy, or organic social in an ecommerce brand.
steps: Accept the mechanism: generic AI output ('slop') exists because models share training data, so asking AI to invent angles produces the same answers your competitors get.

Manually author and store your proprietary raw material: founder origin stories, specific product-development failures, customer conversations, manufacturing decisions, strong opinions about the category. The source calls this your 'unmade dataset'.
Keep it in a structured, searchable place — a living brand document or content library — so it can be pasted into prompts as context.
Restrict AI to repeating, remixing, and reformatting that approved material across channels and formats: blog to email to social captions to product page blurbs.
Never let AI originate the net-new thinking or the initial phrasing; the human does the heavy lifting, the machine handles distribution.
Refresh the dataset continuously — every new tested claim, failed test, or customer insight is new proprietary input.
caveats: This is a workflow philosophy from the source, not a tested conversion result.
The quality of AI remixes is capped by the quality and specificity of the raw material you supply.

cards.title: Robots repeat, humans write: split original thinking from distribution
cards.summary: Humans author the initial, validated 'approved language'; AI only re-swizzles and cross-posts it.
cards.use_when: Designing the content production process for an ecommerce brand's blog, email, and social calendar.
steps: Define the human step precisely: drafting the original argument, the tested claim, and the first phrasing. This is the work you never delegate to a model.

Once a piece is approved, treat its language as an asset. Feed it to AI with instructions to remix: shorten for social, expand into an email, turn a paragraph into a carousel script, reformat into a checklist.
Apply one source idea across every channel rather than generating a new idea per channel — this compounds recognition and keeps the message consistent.
Maintain an 'approved language' library: the phrases, claims, and framings AI is allowed to reuse, so remixes stay on-brand.
Batch the remix step separately from the writing step so the human thinking does not get diluted by tool output mid-draft.
caveats: The split is a working rule the source proposes, not a validated performance finding.
AI remixes of long text can drift from your approved claims; review before publishing, especially anything with product or compliance implications.

cards.title: Deconstruct voice into measurable variables so it can be repeated
cards.summary: Voice is not mystical; it is word choice, adjective swapping, sentence length, and rhythmic pacing that you can define and replicate.
cards.use_when: Writing a brand style guide or briefing a writer or AI tool so ecommerce copy sounds consistently like your brand across PDPs, emails, and ads.
steps: Sample 5-10 pieces of your best-performing or most on-brand copy and analyze them on four variables: (1) specific word choice — which nouns and verbs recur; (2) adjective swapping — which descriptors you reach for and which you ban; (3) sentence length — the mix of short punches and longer explanations; (4) rhythmic pacing — where the emphasis lands, how sentences begin and end.
Write those observations into explicit rules with examples: 'Sentences stop at 12 words in benefit lines', 'Never use luxury or premium; say heavy-gauge and hand-finished'.
Convert the rules into a reusable prompt block or style sheet that both human writers and AI remix tools receive every time.
Test consistency by rewriting an old piece under the rules and comparing it to the original — if the new version carries the same feel, the rules are portable.
caveats: Voice deconstruction is the source's method; measured conversion impact is not established.
Over-rigid rules can flatten copy; treat them as defaults with deliberate exceptions for high-stakes pages.

cards.title: Timely vs. timeless: balance the content portfolio for compounding assets
cards.summary: Hyper-timely posts spike for 24 hours and retain nothing; timeless essays compound and feed the brand brain for years.
cards.use_when: Allocating the content calendar between trend-jacking social posts and durable resources for an ecommerce store.
steps: Sort planned content into timely (reactive posts, trend commentary, event tie-ins) and timeless (evergreen guides, category explainers, definitive takes on the problem your product solves).
Expect the source's stated pattern: timely content gets a high short spike and near-zero long-term retention; timeless content steadily accumulates and can be reused indefinitely.
Keep timely output for reach and cultural relevance, but do not let it consume the budget that produces durable assets.
Design each timeless piece to be re-usable: it should be quotable in emails, excerptable on product pages, and re-postable in edited form across platforms.
Revisit and update timeless pieces on a schedule instead of writing new ones — updates extend the compounding rather than resetting it.
caveats: The 24-hour spike / long-term retention contrast is the source's characterization, not a measured benchmark.
Timely content can drive real short-term sales spikes (drops, launches); the warning is about relying on it as the foundation.

cards.title: Point of view as a moat: force competitors into catch-up mode
cards.summary: A proprietary methodology or lens is the defensible asset in the AI era — not the software or the content volume.
cards.use_when: Defining positioning for a new product line, brand story, or category entry, or responding to a competitor copying your copy.
steps: Identify the lens only your brand can hold: a specific method, sourcing philosophy, or belief about how the category should work that most competitors would not or could not adopt.
State it as a repeatable methodology with named steps or principles, not a slogan — the source frames a point of view as proprietary software for thinking.
Apply the lens consistently across product development decisions, product pages, and content so every output reinforces it.
Treat competitor imitation as a signal the lens is working; the source argues a distinct point of view forces rivals into perpetual catch-up because they cannot claim the same tested position.
Use the lens as a filter for partnerships, products, and content topics — anything that contradicts it dilutes the moat.
caveats: The 'perpetual catch-up' framing is the source's argument, not measured competitive data.
A point of view only functions as a moat if it is backed by consistent execution the competitor cannot credibly copy.
cards.source_name: The Right Way To Write With AI.docx

cards.title: Language is open source: ownership comes from repetition and association
cards.summary: Vocabulary and common sentence patterns are public domain, so you cannot own words — only the associations you build through volume and repetition.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to trademark-style your messaging, panic about copied copy, or plan long-term brand language investment.
steps: Accept that any phrase you write can be reused by anyone; there is no proprietary claim over letters, words, or common combinations.
Shift investment from invention of novel vocabulary to consistent repetition: use your key phrases across every channel, product page, and email until they are associated with you.
Pick a small set of signature terms for products, methods, or values and repeat them verbatim rather than paraphrasing each time.
Measure association over volume and time, not originality per instance — the source's mechanism is repetition, not cleverness.
Do not chase one-off viral phrasing; build a repeatable lexicon and use it until it becomes the category's shorthand for your approach.
caveats: The 'language as open source' framing is the source's mental model, not a legal position — trademark and IP law still apply to names and marks.
Repetition without substance can read as empty marketing; pair it with the specific unmade details from the personality tier.
cards.source_name: The Right Way To Write With AI.docx

cards.title: Build a company brain content library before automating distribution
cards.summary: Companies need dedicated writers/thinkers to build a central content library that feeds automated social pipelines, instead of generating posts ad hoc.
cards.use_when: Standing up or restructuring a content operation for an ecommerce brand, especially before investing in scheduling or AI distribution tools.
steps: Dedicate at least one role (internal or contracted) to authoring and maintaining the central library of approved language: claims, stories, viewpoints, product truths.
Structure the library so it can be consumed by both humans and automation: tagged by topic, format-agnostic, with the raw specifics (numbers, dates, failures) intact.
Only then wire up distribution — automated social posting, email repurposing, or AI reformatting — pulling from the library rather than generating from scratch.
Keep a human owner accountable for library quality; automating distribution of weak source material just scales commodity slop.
Review the library on a cadence and retire or update material that is outdated or no longer matches the brand's point of view.
caveats: The source frames this as enterprise infrastructure advice; small stores can run a lightweight version of the same pattern in a single document.
Automation without an authored source library reproduces the exact generic content the framework warns against.
